items.content_html:
Short Story - Fantasy / Horror

Chapter 4

Looking at Mrs. Raven’s dead body, Mr. Wolfe scratched his head and murmured. “Okay, I might be wrong.”

“Well, she did that to herself,” people standing around said.

“Yeah. I’ll bury her.” Mr. Wolfe carried her body into the woods.

The day after Mrs. Raven was murdered, thirteen bodies were found; an unprecedented number. What was more disturbing was that they were arranged in a circle like a ritual.

Mr. Goad and Mr. Wolfe sent more people to the guillotine. Fifteen. Twenty the next day. And yet more and more bodies were found the next morning.

Mrs. Fowler was found floating in the river. “A faithful Christian like her… God’s wrath…” Mr. Goad almost lost his mind. He ordered all the men who had participated in the water test to be executed.

“Mr. Goad, not many people left. We’ll have to send mothers or their children to the machine if we want more,” Mr. Wolfe said. “And… Maybe that’s indeed not a good idea. I mean… Maybe… maybe she was right.”

“Maybe… But if it’s necessary…”

“Mrs. Donker is still finding more names.”

Mr. Goad buried his head in his hands. “This demon is… different.”

“It is. Mr. Goad, I suggest you carry your cross all the time. As a Holy Man, a prophet, the regular demon might not be able to go near you. But I have a feeling this one might be stronger just a bit.”

“You might be right. You might just be right.”

Mr. Wolfe gulped, trembling a little. “Mr. Goad, I just realized something.”

“What thing?”

“All… all the people either killed by this monster or executed are…”

“What? Speak.”

“…are those who supported the decision six years ago. Is it a coincidence… or a punishment?”

“Nonsense.” Mr. Goad’s voice was weak. “That’s nonsense.”

“Okay. Mr. Goad, I’ll go home now. You take care.”

* * *

In bed, Mr. Goad held the cross tightly. He was very tired but too anxious to fall asleep, like a windmill that wanted to stop but the strong wind kept spinning it. Exhaustion would overcome him every five to ten seconds, but then he would jump and hold the cross even tighter.    

“Tomorrow, we start with the five mothers and their ten kids at the eastern part of the village. I’ll find the demon. I’ll keep my reputation.”

Suddenly, something blew out the candle. It was pitch black. “Ah!” He was shaking.

Absolute silence.

He saw a shadow slowly moving in the room. It split into dozens of shadows and started dancing and singing. Some had blurry faces, and they were smiling. He recognized a few of them. The bigger they smiled, the more horrified he was. Behind all the shadows there was a fire. It was just a dim light in the beginning but grew brighter and brighter, casting more shadows from the shadows.

He closed his eyes and raised the cross up high, screaming at the top of his lungs, “Begone! Devil! Begone!”

When he opened his eyes, the cross turned into a piece of wood with thick brown stains. It was from the guillotine. He shrieked and threw it away.   

All went dark. Silence again.

A black cat appeared at the window. It lightly and elegantly jumped to the end of the bed. The moment she touched the bed, she turned into Mrs. Raven.

“No,” he said, shaking his head.

“I’m not here to judge,” she said.

“What?”

Then he was on the guillotine, looking at Mr. Goad, who was smiling. He realized he was all the countless people he himself had ordered to be imprisoned or executed, all at once. He was the teen girl, separated from her parents and family, terrified and crying, thrown into solitary confinement. “No!” He tried but couldn’t break free. Suddenly he was deep in the water. Looking up, he saw his reflection, but it was Mrs. Raven’s despairing face.

Slowly, his eyes finally closed.   

* * *

The news of Mr. Goad’s death spread like plague. Mrs. Donker screamed and screamed, tearing her clothes and pulling her hair out. She went insane, walking half-naked from then on.

With no one left to order executions, the village became dead quiet. Those who survived, mostly women and children, scrambled to make ends meet. The skilled women gathered what was left: livestock, crops, tools, and anything available to rebuild the village.

* * *

A month after the death of Mr. Goad.

It was a sunny but somewhat chilly afternoon. Mr. Wolfe walked up a tall hill, looking over the endless forest.

A shadow approached him. When it was right behind him, he smiled without turning around. “Raven.”

“Wolf.” Raven came to stand right next to him, looking over the forest with him.

They were quiet for a long while. The wind started to pick up. Wolf squinted, feeling the gusts on his face. Raven raised her head high and extended her arms like flying.

“Do you smell that?” Wolf said, smiling.

“Yeah?”

“Grass. The mud around the lake. The oaks and birches. No blood.”

“No blood. We gave them so many chances, didn’t we?”

“That we did. You did. I just made sure innocent blood was avenged.”

Another quiet moment.  

“Was it a little close? Just a little?” Raven said. “They knew the only way to kill us.”

“We’ve been doing this for thousands of years.”

She looked at him.

“Then it’ll be just five hundred years of sleep. A blink of an eye.”

“You don’t know that. No one has been resurrected.”

“Yet.”

She smirked, then whispered, “Death is a little long for me.”

He locked eyes with her, his hand resting on her arm. “Not in the eye of eternity.”

She touched his back. He smiled at her. “It’s nothing to be afraid of. I’ve heard it’s beautiful; so beautiful, the problem is you might not want to come back. And it’s another beginning. Life never ends, even for us.”

She slowly exhaled.

“Anyhow, it’s all over, Raven. Let’s keep feeling the sun and the wind.”

“Don’t you see the sky? It’s so blue today.”

They closed their eyes and felt the wind blowing past their torsos.

Wolf said, “Plus, if something really happens to us, someone will continue the work.”

Another shadow walked up the hill.

“Speaking of the devil. Or monster. Mr. Owler,” Raven greeted. “So glad to see you. Welcome.”

Mr. Owler’s eyes flashed red for a split second. His tongue ran over his fangs for a while before he asked, puzzled, “What… what’s all this? Why… What am I…?”

Wolf and Raven exchanged a look and smiled.

“Next?” Wolf said.

“There.” Raven eyed another village beyond the forest.

“What’s the situation?”

“Fear, as usual. Not as much killing, but you’ll need to go under this time.”

Wolf and Raven walked down the hill. Mr. Owler hesitated for a moment, then followed along.

- The End -

Short Story - Fantasy / Horror

Chapter 3

More heads were cut off, and more people died during the night. Now every morning there would be four or five bodies. No one cared for the fields; the sheep, cows, and horses were running around. Stores were closed.

Except for supervising the beheadings, Mr. Goad now locked himself in his room, murmuring all day while holding a cross against his chest. Mrs. Donker called out names, and most of the names would soon be without heads.

One day, Mr. Goad walked out of his room, watching the bloody head-cutting machine without a word.

“Mr. Goad,” Mr. Wolfe walked by, took off his hat to greet him, then kept walking.

“Mr. Wolfe,” Mr. Goad called.

“Yes, sir?”

“Mr. Doggs mentioned that you both saw the devil?”

“Sure did. We were lucky to be alive.”

“And it looked more like a… monster? Not a spirit?”

“Indeed.”

Mr. Goad sighed. “You mentioned the shape-shifter? A skinwalker?”

Mr. Wolfe lowered his head with an uneasy smile.

“No no, I grant you permission to speak. Loosen your tongue.”   

“Really?” Mr. Wolfe’s eyes sparkled. “You would listen?”

“As true as I’m the mouthpiece of the Lord.”

“Okay! Okay! Where do I start? Yes, my old mama, God rest her soul, taught me about the shape-shifters and skinwalkers when I was a kid… They ain’t afraid of daylight. My old mama loved cooking, right? And at dinner every day, she would prepare…”

“Skip the mama part, please.”

“Oh, but it’s related. My old mama would prepare three dishes, a lot of corn, and so she’d go to the field, and…” Looking at Mr. Goad’s face, he said, “…and the shape-shifters like to change their forms; well, obviously, as their name indicates, haha. They like to live among people, you know? They kill for energy, but also absorb it from sunlight. Oh, and they run lightning fast like hell! In the blink of an eye they’re in front of you now, heya!” He jumped. “Now, how do they kill, you ask? Well, they do have fangs like vampires, but shorter. But usually they just shock the victims, and they die in a second. Foolproof.”

“That’s why no blood, no injury.”

“That’s why. Now, how to kill them, you ask. The best way is to drown them, then bury them deep in…”

“No no, Mr. Wolfe, you’re misinformed. I know little about monsters of this kind, but one thing I’m certain of is how to kill one…” He stroked his goatee. “Decapitation is the only way.”

“Oh.” Mr. Wolfe raised an eyebrow, then pulled his hat down and lowered his head.

“So we’re doing the right thing, just need to find the right person.”

“I see, Holy Man.”

“How about skinwalkers?”

“They’re pretty much the same, except they fly. Oh, both shape-shifters and skinwalkers have red eyes.”

“I see. Thank you, Mr. Wolfe. Valuable information. Now the question is which demon we’re dealing with right now. How do we know?”

Mr. Wolfe scratched his head. “Mama didn’t say… After all, they all change shapes. They can be human now, the next minute a bird, then a cat…”

“We’ll have to cast a bigger net then.”

“Of course. So, what are you going to do? I’d like to help if that suits you.”

Mr. Goad closed his eyes and prayed, “Oh Lord, show me thy way. You have shown me who to trust and who to punish before, who to love and who to hate, who to blame and put away. Now give me the wisdom again, I beg thee, Lord.”

They stood there for a while. Mr. Wolfe didn’t know what to do; he touched his hat and watched a few people walk by.

“Yes, Mr. Wolfe.” Mr. Goad opened his eyes. “The Lord’s will has been revealed to me. I’ll appoint you to be my counsel.”

“Me… me?”

“Yes. The job might be intimidating; it’s not for the faint-hearted. May the Lord give you strength.”

“Why, yes! Yes! Mr. Goad, thank you for trusting me with such an important job!”

“It’s a calling.”

“Yes, such an important calling! I’m honored! Oh, what about Mrs. Donker?”

“What about her?”

“She’s the one giving the names.” Mr. Wolfe raised his hands. “But I happen to agree with all her inspirations.”

“Yes, yes, she’s a faithful Christian. You can work with her.”

“And Mrs. Fowler. They were big supporters of your big decision six years ago. What pure souls they are.”

“Indeed. Now, come to my worship room this afternoon, let’s discuss more names.”

“Will do, sir.”

Mr. Goad and Mr. Wolfe decided on ten names. It was a big number, yes, but it was better be safe than sorry. The next morning, no corpses were found. They had another ten names. Again, a peaceful morning.

“Have we caught the demon?” Mr. Goad asked.

“Possibly, but if we’re as careful and smart as my old mama, we know the demon can transform into another form when we don’t notice.”

“We should keep finding more names then.”

“I think so.”

Mr. Goad frowned. “At this rate, the village will be empty pretty soon.”

Mr. Wolfe scratched his head. “Oh.”

“Hmm.”

“Should we stop then?”

Mr. Goad touched his goatee. “No. We can’t let the demon win. Even if that means some sacrifice has to be made.”

“I see.”

Someone knocked on the door. “C’mon in. Oh, why, Mrs. Raven!” Mr. Goad rushed to welcome her with a smile that couldn’t be bigger and sweeter. “Why do I have the honor of your visit?” He held her hand.

“Ah, all the blood!” She sat down, touched her forehead, and closed her eyes. “When is it going to stop?”

“Now, the demon is cunning, we mustn’t let it get away. Even if that means some sacrifice has to be made.” Mr. Wolfe nodded with satisfaction, then looked at Mr. Goad for approval. And approval he got.

But Mrs. Raven stared at Mr. Wolfe with an intensity that could ignite a fire. “Such cruelty, such nonsense! I wouldn’t hear any of it! How dare you, Mr. Wolfe? Who are you to think a merciful God would grant you the right to do such things? A God who feeds the hungry, gives water to the thirsty, welcomes the strangers, clothes the naked, cares for the sick, and visits those imprisoned? How dare you?”

“I… No, I mean…” Mr. Wolfe’s face turned white.

“Dear Mrs. Raven, you shouldn’t let such worries pollute your purity. It’s a man’s job. A woman with such rare beauty shouldn’t be mad like this.”

“I’d be mad at whatever I see fit. Now, I came here to negotiate.”

“Negotiate?”

“I’ve learned something about demons and monsters myself. They ain’t capable of transforming into children. They might possess children, maybe, like what you claimed six years ago. But they can’t transform into children. So I forbid you to send any children to prison. Not to mention sending them to their end.”

“They ain’t capable?” Mr. Wolfe said.

“They ain’t!” She yelled.

Right, okay, they ain’t.”

“Also, their parents must be spared. At least their mothers.”

“Why?” Mr. Goad asked.

“Who would care for the children then? You?”

“Right.”

“And I forbid you to send more people to their end just because they’re not local.”

“But they’re evil. They take away villagers’ jobs and make them starve.” Mr. Goad frowned.

“That’s just nonsense! They’re doing the jobs the villagers are too proud to do. Finally, if they were children six years ago, they should be spared too.” 

Mr. Wolfe and Mr. Goad looked at each other.

“These poor kids have been traumatized ever since, thanks to you, Mr. Goad. Has anyone cared about their pain? No! The whole village cheered for it! Those who cheered must answer to the Lord for their crime! And now you want to murder them too? Is God even just anymore?”

“Mrs. Raven, this is just not right. What if they do horrible things now?” Mr. Wolfe asked.

“Then they’ll be judged by their crimes, not by your ‘inspiration.’”

“I don’t think so. This ain’t right. You might as well ask us to spare everyone! That ain’t gonna happen.” Mr. Wolfe shook his head.

Mrs. Raven burst into tears. “Mr. Wolfe! You insult the merciful Lord! You insult me! I won’t accept any of it! I won’t!”

“Mrs. Raven, be reasonable!” Mr. Wolfe raised his voice. “A woman!”

“A woman!? You feel inferior in front of a woman smarter than you? You feel threatened?”

“I’ll tell you what you should feel now, woman!” Mr. Wolfe shouted.

“Okay, alright, alright,” Mr. Goad said. “Mrs. Raven, we’ll think about it, alright? I promise we’ll think about it.”

“I want his apology!”

“In your dream!” Mr. Wolfe hissed.

“The insult!” She shed more tears. Looking at her tears, Mr. Goad shook his head. “Oh… For heaven’s sake, Mr. Wolfe, just apologize.”

“What? Why?”

“Mr. Wolfe. She’s a delicate flower.”

“…sorry, Mrs. Raven,” He murmured.

After she left, Mr. Goad nodded. “Mr. Wolfe, you have earned more trust in me now. A woman should know her place. Just don’t say it out loud to her.”

“Winning your trust is always my only goal.” Mr. Wolfe bowed to him.

* * *

For a week, only the machine was doing the job. Ten people at a time.

Though there were no more corpses in the morning, Mrs. Raven’s proposal caused almost the same level of disturbance and quarrels. It didn’t help her that more and more men became upset because they couldn’t get her to give them enough attention. They had had enough of her “No, thank you” or “No.” Many of them were married, sure, but that didn’t justify her rejection. After all, they were very nice to her, she should know she was obligated to reciprocate, they claimed.

Someone knocked on Mr. Goad’s door. A group of men and women, including Mrs. Donker and Mrs. Fowler, came in.

“What’s the matter?” Mr. Goad asked.

“Mr. Goad, have you thought about the unthinkable?” Mrs. Donker said.

“What do you mean?”

“Could it be Mrs. Raven?”

People around her looked at each other and nodded.

“Why?”

“Well, first of all, a beautiful woman like her shouldn’t be trusted.”

“I agree!” Mrs. Fowler said.

“Not to mention the idea of sparing everyone! She must be working with the demon! Or she’s the demon herself!” Some men shouted.

“Yes! She’s the demon!” Others chimed in.

Mr. Wolfe slapped his own forehead. “Oh no, that’s right!”

“What’s right?” Mr. Goad asked.

“If I know what my mama taught me, she’s no shape-shifter or skinwalker; they prefer to mingle with the crowd rather than turn into someone with such a prominent appearance. The smell ain’t right too. She’s not the demon—but a witch who works with them!” He yelled the last part. Pausing for a few seconds to enjoy being the center of attention, he continued, “We should do the water test!”

“Water test! We need to kill the witch!” Mrs. Donker shouted.

“We need to kill her! Swim the witch!” Mrs. Fowler followed.

“Swim the witch! Kill the witch!” Everyone chanted. “Swim the witch! Kill the witch!”

Mr. Goad nodded. “Valuable information, valuable indeed! Let’s swim a witch!”

Mrs. Raven was brought to the river. All the men who were rejected by her before were staring at her, smirking.

“Mrs. Raven,” Mr. Goad announced with authority. “You came to my worship place the other night and made some outrageous proposals. I was fooled by you then. But God will not be mocked. You are to be tied up and sunk into the river. If you float, you’re the witch because the water of baptism rejects you. If you sink, you’re innocent. May God have mercy on your evil soul.”

“You!” Mrs. Raven roared. “All you people! I negotiated to spare the lives of so many of you! And this is how you repay me? Is this what your God teaches you? Hypocrisy? Greed for power? Murder? Where’s love and turning the other cheek?”

“One has only so many cheeks to turn,” one man said coldly.

She was stripped to her undergarments. Many men were gawking, commenting, and mocking. Then they tied her up and fastened a rope around her waist.

Mr. Wolfe sneered at her. “We’ll see if you’re a witch.” He pushed her into the water.

She sank.

Short Story - Fantasy / Horror

Chapter 2

When two more bodies were found the next day, Mr. Goad ordered the guillotine to be brought out and displayed at the plaza in front of the village house. “It was revealed to me last night by the Holy Spirit that the evil spirit is able to turn itself into human form. It’s time to catch and execute the evil among us!” He loudly claimed.

“The evil spirit is among us?” Mr. Hipol said.

“Just like six years ago. Only at that time, they possessed humans instead of becoming one.”

“How did you know it’s not possessing this time?” Mr. Hipol asked.

Mr. Goad scornfully said, “As I mentioned, because six years ago we cleansed up all the possessive evil spirits, of course. I cleansed them all up.”

“By imprisoning children and shedding innocent blood.” Mr. Olwer said.

“Nonsense!” Mr. Goad interrupted, his cane hit on the guillotine so loudly that everyone was startled. “Every. Single. One. Of. Them. Was. Justly. Imprisoned. Or. Executed!! They were weak-minded; they allowed the devilish lust, the dirty desire for carnal knowledge to pollute their thoughts, surrendering themselves to temptation! As true as God lives, I was right and the whole village cheered for me! The whole village! Every single villager!”

“When will we have peace?” Mrs. Donker cried.

“I just think our merciful and all-powerful Lord wouldn’t want us to make more mistakes if we can prevent it, right?” Mr. Owler said.

“That’s right! That’s why we must find the spirit and kill it now!” Mrs. Donker said.

“No! That’s not what I meant…” Mr. Owler tried to be louder.

“We need to do something quick!” Mrs. Fowler said.

“Indeed, rightfully so!” Mr. Goad cleared his throat and announced, “From now on, if you see anyone acting suspicious, come to me! I’ll be in my worship room praying.”

* * *

In less than one hour, someone knocked on Mr. Goad’s door.

“C’mon in. Oh, Mr. Ante, what can I help you with today?”

Mr. Ante was a hatter with a big mustache. “I believe I saw the evil spirit, sir. See, last night I was walking down the street minding my own business, and I think I saw the cook from that big house, you know? I don’t know, he just looked guilty, like the way he walked wasn’t like, the way a God-fearing guy should walk, you know?”

“The cook, huh? Hmm, interesting.”

“Yeah, yeah. And see, he isn’t local and he misses church.” Mr. Ante shrugged with open palms. “That’s suspicious enough, no?”

“True, true! Valuable information, Mr. Ante! Valuable, indeed.”

Two hours later, the cook was dragged to the public and had his head cut off, amid people’s shouting and cursing. Mr. Goad grinned and nodded with approval. “Well done. Now we shall live in peace.”

People cheered. Mr. Owler stood away from the crowd, shaking his head.

* * *

It wasn’t comforting at all when the villagers found three more bodies in the woods the very next morning. They were near the lake. No blood, no injury. Only some mud on their bodies and faces.

“How… how many evil spirits are there?” Mr. Wolfe asked, trembling.

“Mr. Goad, what should we do?” Mrs. Donker pleaded.

Mr. Goad stared at the guillotine for a moment. “Mr. Ante, did you see what you thought you saw that night?”

“Sure did!”

“What did you see?”

“The cook walked on the street, acting all suspicious.”

“And what was the crime again?”

“The… the way he walked. Suspicious and all that. And not attending church. Oh, and he was not from here, see.”

“So, what were you doing when seeing him?”

“Walked… walked down the street.”

“At night?”

Mr. Ante’s eyes widened. “Hey, hey now…”  

People turned to stare at him.

“Wicked devil, you think you could fool a prophet twice!?” Mr. Goad shouted with unmistakable authority.

“It’s him! It’s him!” Everyone shouted.

Mr. Ante’s head was cut off.

“Now, go home and pray,” Mr. Goad ordered. “So our Lord have mercy on your souls.”

“Praise the Lord!” Mrs. Donker said.

“We shall have peace now, thank you, Mr. Goad.” Mrs. Fowler said.

“I should go home and rest, have a long overdue good sleep.” Mr. Hipol wiped his face.

Mr. Owler scanned the crowd. Mr. Wolfe was cleaning his shoes while begging people around to pray with him.

* * *

That night, Mr. Goad studied scriptures with good effort. His reading skills were somehow limited, but enough to interpret the Holy Bible, or at least say something about it. He was digging deep into the book, trying to find more authority to claim.

Someone knocked on the door. “C’mon in.”

It was Mrs. Donker. “Mr. Goad, I trust you, our prophet, with all my heart. I don’t doubt you a bit. You’re God’s messenger, that’s as true as day.”

“…But?”

“I mean, what if… what if Mr. Ante wasn’t the only evil spirit? Or, what if the evil spirit transformed into another person before Mr. Ante was beheaded?”

“Hmm. Why do you think that?”

“I’m just afraid tomorrow morning we’ll find more bodies. In case we do, I talked to some other villagers, and we all agreed the shepherd with the big nose could be it.”

“Why?”

“Did you know when his wife died, he didn’t even cry? Mrs. Fowler even swore that she saw him smile once.”

“No love in his heart, yes, that could be it.”

“Praise the Lord.”

“Now, Mrs. Donker,” Mr. Goad said, looking around before holding her hand. “You’re safe with me.”

“Ah, Mr. Goad. You’re too lovely.”

* * *

The next morning, people searched around and found no dead bodies. They danced and sang, hailing Mr. Goad as a hero. “It was Mr. Ante!” “Of course! He never sat right with me!”

But just half an hour after sunset, a woman’s scream shook everyone. Right next to a well was the wife of a blacksmith. Though in her forties, she was as strong as her husband. Yet she obviously hadn’t even put up a fight.

“What happened? Didn’t you say all is well now? I just saw her ten minutes ago! Now she’s dead!” Mrs. Fowler asked Mr. Goad.

“I… uh…”

“It’s Mr. Wolfe!” A man shouted. Everyone turned to the voice.

It was Mr. Owler.

Mr. Wolfe’s face turned white. “No… please… I beg everyone to pray with me every day!” He looked as though he might puke at any second. “I don’t even eat pork! I don’t even know what’s going on. Are there evil spirits? A shape-shifter? A skinwalker? My old mama taught me they ain’t afraid of daylight when I was a kid…”

“Where were you just five minutes ago?” Mr. Owler questioned.

“I went to take a piss and shit.”

“He’s about to shit himself again,” some laughed.

“How did you know it was him?” Mr. Hipol asked.

“The three bodies found near the lake had mud on them. I saw Mr. Wolfe cleaning mud off his shoes!”

Mrs. Raven, who stood and observed quietly, let out a sigh. Though soft, half of the men turned to her. “What’s the matter, Mrs. Raven?”

“The blacksmith’s wife was a good friend of mine. I still owe her two coins. She was such a nice and strong woman.”

“Aye.”

“Everybody, listen! I’m sure it’s Mr. Wolfe!” Mr. Owler said.

Mr. Wolfe’s face was now grey. He whimpered and was about to bawl. “Please… Have mercy… I pray every day… Mrs. Donker, you know me well, speak for me!”

“No, Mr. Wolfe ain’t it. I don’t see it.” Mrs. Donker shook her head. “It’s someone else. I know.”

“Nah. Mr. Wolfe had no clue; he even asked how many evil spirits were there,” Mrs. Fowler added.

People mocked Mr. Owler. “You and your woo-woo knowledge are no good at finding an evil spirit!” “The woo-woo knowledge is no good at anything!”

“It’s the shepherd!” Mrs. Donker claimed, pointing a finger at him. “I knew it all along!”

“I agree!” Mrs. Fowler followed. “Kill him!”

“Right! Right, the one without love in heart, how could I forget?” Mr. Goad cried.

“You guys are mistaken!” Mr. Owler yelled.

“Help!” The shepherd cried.

The shepherd’s head was cut off.

That night, no one slept with their eyes closed.

* * *

Finally, the morning came. People went out to search for bodies. They didn’t find any. The next two days were the same.

“So… It really was the shepherd?” People were more cautious, looking at each other.

“It was the shepherd! I was right!” Mrs. Donker gladly claimed.

“And I too!” Mrs. Fowler followed.

“So glad this is over,” Mrs. Raven was panting, about to faint. “I can’t stand all the deaths and blood. Too cruel.”

At least six men stood by her side, comforting her. “It’s over now, don’t be afraid,” a man said.

“Anyone who wants to hurt you will answer to my fist first.” The man saying that flexed his fist and bicep while looking at her heaving chest.

* * *

That night, believing it was safe now, Mr. Wolfe had Mr. Doggs, an old brewer, walk with him across the village to collect some stones. Mr. Doggs was a notorious gossip; all the stories, real or fake, would be broadcast by him.

“Mr. Doggs, I’ve heard Mrs. Donker and Mr. Goad know each other a little too well?”

“Sheesh!” Mr. Doggs covered his mouth and looked around. “There are things not supposed to be said out loud!”

“Oh, I’m sorry, truly sorry… I won’t say a word.”

“Not out loud, just whisper.”

“Oh.”

“You heard right.”

“I was right?”

“Yeah.”

Mr. Wolfe waited for ten seconds. “… that’s it?”

Mr. Doggs shrugged. “Mr. Goad is a powerful man.”

“Of course. Is Mrs. Donker the only…”

“Sheesh!” He covered his mouth again.

“Okay, I’m not sure what is okay and what is not…” He muffled.

“No! You hear that?”

“Hmm?”

They both looked around. “There…” Mr. Wolfe’s face turned white. He whispered, “There seems to be… some breathing…”

Suddenly, a shadow jumped over their heads, screeching and laughing before it disappeared. “Ah!” They both screamed.

“Run!” Mr. Wolfe grabbed Mr. Doggs’s arm and ran for their lives.

* * *

Imagine the shock and discouragement when the villagers found two more bodies the next morning.

They were Mr. Hipol and Mr. Owler.

items.content_html:
Short Story - Fantasy / Horror

Chapter 1

It was an especially dark night, the moon was hidden behind a thick cloud. A middle-aged man walked through the woods, carrying a torch. He had a bushy beard and a bald head. He was mumbling to himself: “I should have got two more silver coins for that. After all, if someone has to cheat to be rich, it should be me…”

Suddenly, he heard a strange noise. It was brief and soft like leaves rustling, but something about it got him curious. “What is it?” he murmured.

Then he noticed how quiet it was. “Someone’s there?”

The quietness became eerie now, like a thick cloud pouring down on his head. “Show thyself!”

He didn’t even have time to blink, a shadow jumped on him. He fell without making a sound.

* * *

 “You found him this morning?”

The next day just a little before noon, three men were standing around the dead man’s body. The one in the middle who spoke was Mr. Goad, a short old man with a long face. His mustache and goatee were white as snow, and his small eyes always looked at people with skepticism.

“Yes sir,” the man on his left said. “This morning I was on my way to the market, and he was lying there face down. He must have seen something that didn’t agree with him. Poor fella.”

“And this is the fourth death this week. All without a good reason: no injury, no sign of fights.” Mr. Goad lightly hit the body with his black heavy cane.

“That must be a vampire,” the man on Mr. Goad’s right said. “He was killed by a vampire.”

“Beg your pardon?” Mr. Goad frowned.

“All his blood was sucked dry! Don’t you see?” His trembling finger pointed at the body. “Look at his neck, aren’t there two holes?”

Mr. Goad and the first man took a closer look at the body. “He doesn’t look dry to me,” the first man said, moving the corpse’s head around to check his neck. “And I don’t see no holes.”

“Then what is that?” The second man pointed at a small red spot on the body’s right side of the neck.

“That’s just a red spot… a rash?” the first man said.

“Well, that’s a sign of a vampire’s attack!” The second man insisted.

“And you know that’s a sign of a vampire’s attack because…” the first man asked.

“Because he was killed by a vampire!”

The first man scratched his head. “I’m not sure…”

“This was no vampire,” Mr. Goad sniffed. “I’ve seen so many cases like this I lose count. I can smell them from a mile away.”

“What is it, then?” the first man asked.

Mr. Goad stroked his goatee. “Evil spirit, son. Evil spirit. I’ve met this kind before, during the day it hid in caves or trees, and at night it’ll come out, pick an unfortunate soul and take it away from the rightful owner just for fun.”

The second man gulped. “That’s nothing nicer than a vampire. Not a bit.”

“I’ve sent countless possessed peasants to jail or the guillotine. I know how to take matters like this into my own hands. You watch, sons; you just watch.” He patted them both on their shoulders. “We’ve got ourselves a war... but I’m going to put an end to it. By putting a rope around the evil spirit’s neck.”

“Mr. Goad, you don’t think this to be the wrath from God, do you?” the first man asked.

“Why on earth do you think that?” Mr. Goad hissed.

“That thing we did a few years ago…”

Mr. Goad cleared his throat. “Nonsense. This is no wrath from God. We did nothing wrong. This is an evil spirit.”

“What should we do?” the second man asked.

“Let’s go tell the village head, tell him to get everyone together.” Mr. Goad raised his head.

* * *

This tiny village had less than two hundred people. The village head, Mr. Hipol, was a big man in his late forties. For some reason his face was always red, and he perspired a lot, even when he wasn’t moving around. He rarely made a decision. In his own words, he liked to wait till things “straighten themselves out.”

Mr. Hipol gathered all the villagers for a meeting in the village house. The news already spread like fire. Though it was a particularly warm day, everyone felt a chill breath down their necks, making them shiver. “What happened?”

“A man was killed last night!”

“What, another one!?”

“They said these people were all killed by werewolves!”

“No, it was zombies, they were eaten alive!”

“Their skulls were crushed and brains spilled all over!”

“Mr. Hipol, what should we do? Should we run now? Where?” Mrs. Donker shouted.

Mrs. Donker was in her thirties. She was a small woman with pale skin, but her voice was as loud as her fire-red hair.

“I… I don’t…” Mr. Hipol stuttered and shook his head hard.

“No need to panic, my good people!” Mr. Goad yelled. “Have four people died mysteriously? Yes. Were they killed by some creature of monstrous nature? Indeed. Is the devil still among us? Definitely. Will it kill again? Most likely. But have I let any evil spirits and witches escape from justice? Never!” He waved his cane.

“What does it want anyway? Maybe if we give it what it wants it’ll go away!” Mrs. Donker said. Many people nodded.

“Now, now, my people, you can’t reason with the devil. It’s the enemy of all mankind and it wants to destroy every single soul on earth. That’s what it wants,” Mr. Goad said. “But never underestimate the power of faith and prayer. Here, let’s pray together to chastise the devil and resist its control. Repeat after me.” He put down his cane and raised his arms high, citing the scripture: “Submit yourselves, then, to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.”

Everyone repeated.

“There shall no evil befall thee. For he shall give his angels charge over thee.”

Repeated again.

“See, feel the Lord’s protection now?”

Silence.

Seeing people’s faces, he raised his cane. “Did I mention my cane has holy power too? It’s helped me so many times to chase down witches and monsters. Tonight I’m going to use my cane combined with the power our Lord gives me to protect us. Go home, or do whatever is necessary. But when the sun sets, lock your door and do not go out and about. I say: do not go out. Stay inside and pray like a good man. The spirit won’t be able to hurt you and I promise that’s true.”

“And you’ll hunt it down?” Mrs. Donker asked.

“As sure as I live and breathe.” Mr. Goad nodded.

After everyone left, Mr. Hipol asked Mr. Goad, “People will be safe, right?”

“I trust myself and I have the power. Now if you excuse me, I have a whole village of people to protect.” He knocked his cane on a table and proudly walked out of the door. 

* * *

The next day, another body was found near the forest. It was an old rich widow. Again, no sign of injury or struggle.

Everyone gathered at the village house again, yelling, crying, and praying. “Mr. Goad, where’s your power of protection?” Mrs. Donker shrieked.

Mr. Goad cleared his throat. “Well, didn’t I tell you not to go out and about? What was she doing out there after dark?”

“I thought she was blind and stayed home all the time?” Mr. Hipol said.

“So it’s her fault?” Mrs. Donker asked.

“As surely as there is a hell. I know the Lord is just. He won’t let bad things happen to good people.”

A tanned woman in her late twenties raised her hand. “Yes, Mrs. Fowler,” Mr. Goad said.

Mrs. Fowler was a hard-working farmer; one could always see her in the field with a tool in her hand. She said, “Won’t bad things sometimes happen to good people? My neighbor was a nice old lady and we all loved her dearly, but she died of a horrible disease nobody knew what.”

“Then God had a purpose for her. There’s a purpose for everything and a reason for everything that happens. Or, maybe she did some bad things without us knowing; didn’t you know a righteous man’s good deeds can’t save him once he commits a crime? No worries, as long as you do not surrender to any temptation, you will be fine.”

“Thank you, Mr. Goad, for your wisdom.” Mrs. Fowler put one hand on her chest.

“But the widow was blind and lived a quiet life…” Some murmured.

“We believe you, Mr. Goad!” Mrs. Fowler claimed loudly.

“I still don’t feel safe, Mr. Goad,” Mr. Hipol said, wiping sweat from his face.

“Do something then, aren’t you the village head?” Another guy said.

“No no, no one does anything but me. Only people with authority, with the key to the preshood, like myself, can deal with it.” Mr. Goad tapped his cane. “Now, we need to determine what exactly it is. It’s an evil spirit, that’s established, but of what kind?”

“Could it be a devil in a teen girl’s form, like before?” Mrs. Donker said. “She was especially deceiving!”

“We’ve cleansed the spirits of their power to possess people under my guidance already.” Mr. Goad touched his goatee. “But an evil spirit somehow manifested in a child’s form… that’s not unheard of.”

“Should we round up children?” Mr. Hipol asked.

Mr. Goad pondered for a while. He opened his mouth to speak, nodding, “Maybe we indeed…”

A woman’s scream from outside shocked everyone. People rushed out to investigate and saw the woman lying on the ground with her eyes closed. “Mrs. Raven! Are you alright?” People helped her to sit up.

“Mrs. Raven, did you see something?” “Mrs. Raven, did anybody try to hurt you?” “Mrs. Raven, let me help you!” People, especially men, eagerly expressed their concerns. It probably was because Mrs. Raven was an attractive woman. No one could truly tell how old she was; she never revealed her age. They guessed she was between twenty-five and thirty. Her long dark hair and exotic eyes made people want to get her attention. No one had ever seen Mr. Raven, who was supposedly traveling abroad on business and hadn't been home in years.

Mrs. Raven slowly opened her eyes and whispered, “Can I have some water?”

Five men rushed to fetch some water. After she drank a cup, Mrs. Fowler asked, “What happened, Mrs. Raven?”

“I saw a monster of evil nature…” Mrs. Raven trembled. “It went… that way.” She pointed at an abandoned hut about a quarter of a mile away.

Everyone looked at Mr. Goad. He nodded. A bunch of men grabbed whatever they could get and ran toward it. Soon, they carried a body out of the hut. It was a shoemaker in his thirties.

“What, in this broad daylight?” Mrs. Donker gasped.

“How come it didn’t hurt you, Mrs. Raven?” Mr. Owler asked. He was a short man with white hair. A skilled carpenter, he also helped design a corn mill and irrigation system using “woo-woo” knowledge, as villagers called it.

“Well, it must be getting more and more bloodthirsty, but your purity and faith chased it away.” Mr. Goad patted Mrs. Raven’s hand.

“Thank you, Mr. Goad.” Mrs. Raven smiled.

“You’re welcome. Did you see what it looked like?”

“I couldn’t tell, but it might look like an old, ugly man.”

“I see, I see, valuable information.” Mr. Goad nodded. “But we still can’t totally rule out a spirit in a child’s form, the most deceiving kind, somehow manifests itself to…”

A tall man in his twenties interrupted. “What kind of evil spirit dares to show up when the sun is shining? Maybe it’s not an evil spirit? Maybe… a monster like a shape-shifter? A skinwalker? My old mama taught me they ain’t afraid of daylight when I was a kid…”

Mr. Goad hmphed. “Why, Mr. Wolfe, you think you know your supernatural creatures? Better than a Lord-appointed messenger like myself?”

A man with strong arms, Mr. Wolfe worked as a stonemason. He let out a nervous laugh. “No no, Mr. Goad, please, I didn’t mean to offend you. I just offered my humble opinion.”

“I know what I know, and if anyone wants to live, you better listen to me.”

Everyone mumbled, “Yes.”

“Mr. Goad, I feel your holy authority!” Mr. Wolfe quickly followed. “I feel it in my body. You’re a Holy Man.”

“Evil spirits, show thyself!” Mr. Goad shouted, raising both arms and looking at the sky. “Or I’d chase you down and destroy you with the authority given to me from the Lord!”

“Now, Mr. Goad, I think we should take a step back and see this whole thing from a different perspective…” Mr. Owler said.

“Devil, begone!” Mr. Goad waved his fist.

“Devil, begone!” Mrs. Fowler and Mrs. Donker followed. Everyone followed as well.

“Wait, we need to be careful…” But Mr. Owler’s voice was drowned out by the crowd’s chanting.

items.title: The Old, Old Song "To Know Him is to Love Him"--and the Attachment Style
items.summary: Photo by Tehzeeb Kazmi on Unsplash I'd want to talk about this old song, To Know Him is to Love Him (1958) by The Teddy Bears.  Here are the lyrics: To know, know know him, is to love, love, love him Just to see him…
items.content_html:
I'd want to talk about this old song, To Know Him is to Love Him (1958) by The Teddy Bears. 

Here are the lyrics:

To know, know know him, is to love, love, love him

Just to see him smile, makes my life worthwhile

To know, know know him, is to love, love, love him

And I do

I'll be good to him, I'll bring love to him

Everyone says there'll come a day when I'll walk alongside of him

Yes, yes to know him, is to love, love, love him

And I do, I do

(Bridge)

Why can't he see?  

How blind can he be?

Someday he will see

That he was meant for me, oh oh, yes (back to first stanza)

Whenever I listen to this song, I feel a longing of a thousand years for the love I can't never receive; a one-sided, unrequited love.  Relating it to psychological science (sorry, career hazard), this reminds me of the preoccupied romantic attachment style.  Which I've mentioned before.

This is the style when an individual is obsessed with the love interest, puts them on a pedestal, and feels the pain of a thousand fires in every single second for not being able to be with them.  

"Just to see him smile makes my life worthwhile." This statement shows how much she's willing to sacrifice, even dignity, just to get his attention.  In the heat of the passion, a preoccupied individual might even be willing to offer their own lives to their love, despite not knowing them well.  You might think that's ridiculous, but if you understand that their whole identity and self-worth depend on being loved by that particular person, it isn't that crazy anymore.

Preoccupied individuals tend to see others, especially the romantic interest, as the "better" ones, and at the same time see themselves as potentially not worthy.  To prove their worth, they have to have the love they long for.  They'll go to any lengths to get it.

"Everyone says there'll come a day when I'll walk alongside of him." If you take it on the surface value, you might think, "So maybe there are some mutual feelings, otherwise others won't see them as a potential couple." But keep in mind who the narrator is.  

On the other hand, however, this might not be said by a typical preoccupied individual. It has a little sense of entitlement, and preoccupied people are usually less likely to have that.   

This becomes more obvious in the bridge when she starts blaming him for being "so blind." "Why can't you understand?  We're meant to be together!"

A preoccupied individual's heart, at least in the beginning of the relationship when it's full of uncertainties, will scream, "I know I don't deserve your love, but please love me." Instead, this blaming game reminds me of borderline personality.  You know, the movie Fatal Attraction.  The song isn't so extreme, but the idea is a bit like the difference between "Please love me, or I'll die" vs. "Love me, or else."

That said, the whole song still gives me a more preoccupied feel.  Besides what we've mentioned, "To know him is to love him," "I'll be good to him, I'll bring love to him" are all telltale signs as well; the fire that burns so quick and bright, like the world can collapse now and I won't give a dime.  Please love me.

Is this healthy?  Probably not.  Research shows preoccupied individuals are more likely to break up, mostly due to their intensive responses to any possible threats to the relationship ("Are you interested in that man?" "Are you flirting with that woman?").  Yet I find lots of music, media, and other platforms are pushing people in that direction.  They normalize, even glorify, unhealthy styles of relationships.

items.content_html:
When you fight hard enough, sometimes what’s against you can turn to help you

I’m from Taiwan, a small island next to mainland China. With an area of a little more than half of West Virginia, we squeeze a population bigger than Florida. When I was a kid, to get into senior high schools or colleges, one had to pass the annual entrance exams. Many had spent years taking them. I guess in our Asian minds, education is too precious a resource not to be shared by everyone.

When I entered junior high (7th grade in America), the whole grade was divided into 3 sections based on students’ “aptitude:” A, B, and C. Only students in the A section received the “real” intensive education. Those in B were seen as low-achievers, and no one cared about those in C—people simply gave up on them.

I was in A. We went to school at around 7:30, studied till about 4:30 or 5, then stayed for another 2-3 hours for more classes or quizzes. We were supposed to bring 2 “lunch” boxes. After that, many had to go to cram schools for another 2-3 hours, got home at about 10 or 11, did homework till past midnight, went to bed, repeated the cycle the next day. There were no Saturdays, Sundays, Winter break, or Summer vacation. Only study days.

Every day there were quizzes, and if we didn’t reach a standard, the teachers used a big bamboo rod to beat us on our palms, butts, or the back of our thighs. Every day we were black and blue. To make things worse, I sucked big time on the 2 most important subjects: Math, and English.

I was trapped in hell.

I didn’t (still don’t) understand why my classmates still could breathe, laugh, and eat. Every morning I stood at the door with eyes full of tears, begging “Don’t make me go to school.” But my mom had her own problems. What could she do anyway? I found all excuses and lies to be late for school or simply skip it, got more beatings and hard slaps to the face. The administration had meetings about other delinquents and me. I guess I became famous.

Finally, my teacher had had it. He kicked me out to section B. That basically meant no hope of passing the exam; not the first time at least. If I wanted to, I could go to a cram school, spend a shit ton of money, and cram the shit out of it for a year before trying it again. Later I learned from my old classmates that my section A teacher announced to the whole class about me behind my back: “I’m making sure he won’t get into any school.”

I still studied; hard. I didn’t get English, no problem; I memorized sentences, a bunch of them. I wouldn’t give up without a fight.

But after the exam, I shook my head and sighed: well, I tried. Guess I’m stupid and I deserve it.    

That was why when a relative called and told my mom that I got into a high school, even I fell from a chair. I was the only section B “low-achievers” in the whole school who passed the exam.

But in high school, my Math and English still sucked. English was especially interesting: for every class, I simply sat there without absorbing anything, like a rock couldn’t absorb a few tiny drops of water dripping on it. In my senior year, I said to myself: “I’ve got to get into college, and therefore I have to rescue at least one subject.”

For some reason, I thought Math required talents like Einstein, and I surely was hopeless. I decided to work on English—in my own way. For the whole year, after school, I bought dinner home, opened an English book, turned on the radio to English education channels, and struggled. No one was home (long story) so I could concentrate in a quiet environment.

Unfortunately, “the race is not to the swift or the battle to the strong.” Hard work doesn’t guarantee success. Though my English did improve, I didn’t get into any college. I was heartbroken, convinced that people who doubted me were right all along.

I went to mandatory military service for 2 years. Whenever I had private time, I wrote down vocabulary on cards and memorized them. My superior scolded me for that (“Throw away those damn cards and concentrate on your duty!”) and I didn’t remember a lot, but I had the spirit.

After the service, because I was a devoted Christian at that time, I volunteered to be a missionary for 2 years. I had chances to learn English with my American companions. But my inadequate language ability led to many miscommunications and hard feelings. One day I was cooking dinner for my companion and myself, who barely spoke Mandarin. He looked at me: “I hope you’re not putting that egg into the soup.” Too bad I thought he wanted me to do that. He screamed. We rescued that poor egg and didn’t utter another word for the whole night.

After my mission, I fought hard to find a job, but no one cared about a high school graduate except for some sales or labor positions. I either quit the next day or was fired, living under my family’s disappointed eyes. But I never stopped dreaming about college; I applied to our church’s school in Hawaii. A long shot, but I had to try.

Then I found a job as a driver shuttling preschoolers and kindergarteners between the school and their homes. It was the BEST job I’ve ever had in my whole life. I loved the children and they loved me; every morning they hugged me or climbed up on my shoulders. My co-workers were a bunch of the nicest, fun people. Meanwhile, the church urged members to get married ASAP and have 15 kids. In the church there were so many women and so few men, some women had no choice but to hold their noses and close their eyes to consider me. I was so flattered like hell yeah, whatever attention is cool with me.  

I started thinking: maybe I should just settle down?  

And this is the first life lesson I’ve learned: you might not know what exactly you’re gonna be in your life yet, but you should have a basic understanding of what kind of person you are. After careful soul-searching, I came to realize that I was NOT a person who would be happy with a high school diploma, married a woman of faith, had 15 children, opened a small shop, and lived happily ever after—that was NOT me. I didn’t need money or status, but I needed knowledge, I needed to see the world.

A few weeks later, I received an admission letter from the college.

My English continued to stink, but strangely, when it came to things I was enthusiastic about, I just couldn’t shut up. I loved science, I loved astronomy, I loved psychology, so in these classes people could see me talk—sometimes stuttering and sweating, but kept talking. For the classes I cared about (sorry English literature teachers), I previewed the books, maybe recorded the lectures, listened to the whole thing in my room and took more notes, then reviewed again before exams.

My grades were okay, but I struggled with daily conversation. A girl asked me a question, I answered, and she smirked: “That’s not what I’m asking.” I wanted to hide in a cave. A cute red-haired girl invited me to a movie (First Knight starring Richard Gere), I was so shocked and thrilled I nearly passed out. But we walked back to campus under the starry night after the movie—and I could barely utter a coherent sentence. Besides the language barrier, I had NO clue about the dating script in America. I wanted to jump off a cliff.

At least I managed to graduate.

That should have been the end of the story, but I guess I was possessed or what, I dared to start dreaming about graduate schools. As I’ve said in this article, people who knew better tried to put down this idea like swatting a fly. Of course, I didn’t listen. My wife and I went to a small school in Kansas for a counseling degree.

After the first year, however, the professor asked me in our meeting: “What’s going on with you? Every time we talk about your practicum you ‘vibrate’ like that?” Vibrate in this case indicated me being nervous: eyes opening wide, stuttering, sweating, saying “I can’t do it” repeatedly. Wait, I need to talk to people in English? My English?   

I don’t know what I was thinking: it was a counseling degree for heaven’s sake, did I think I’d learn telepathy?  

Then in the Ph.D. program, I saw another mountain too high to climb: the knowledge of research and statistics. Yes, I published a study in a student journal in college, but many others had more impressive accomplishments equipped with a richer statistics background in the program. I didn’t know what I was doing. I knew I wouldn’t last more than a year.

I barely lived through the first semester. But very soon another big challenge hit: I had to deliver a 50-minute lecture to a class of 150. If I had a choice, I’d have said hell no. But it was a demand from a professor.

Oh yeah, I rehearsed the whole lecture from head to toe at least 5 times until I memorized every single word. But what if someone asks a question and I can’t understand what s/he says? Shit, the hell with it; I’d kill myself later.

Luckily, I survived. In fact, I saw some smiles. That day, I realized 2 things:

It doesn’t really matter what you say in the lecture; students don’t pay attention anyway, they just need someone up there talking.

Also: I can teach. And yes, in English.

It was a turning point. Very soon, I learned that by being an instructor I could earn extra cash. The fear of the language was immediately eradicated by the need for $$$. Sign me up!! I screamed. I found my direction. A year later the department head asked me: “What’s your plan after graduation?”

“Teach.” This was NOT in my wildest dreams just a year or 2 before.

People still had their doubts. When I got my Master’s, one of my uncles who got his doctoral degree in America and was a professor in Taiwan took time and money to call me: “You should quit and find a job now.”

“But this is a Ph.D. program.”

“But consider your age; how are you going to raise the whole family? What are you going to do with your life?”

“I’m not gonna give up right now!” And you call me from Taiwan just to tell me that?

The conversation with my mom was amusing: “So what do you do to make money?” she asked. 

“I teach college classes.” 

Paused for a few seconds, she said, “I didn’t know there were Taiwanese there.” 

However, it wasn’t without challenges. For these years in the program, I had to hide my panic in countless classes and meetings because I couldn’t comprehend the terms or slang flying around. After each presentation or defense I endured the humiliation of criticisms that exposed my inadequate knowledge in research and statistics, then went home and admitted to myself that I didn’t belong. I was like a flyless chicken among cranes, and it was time to take off. Who am I kidding?

But miraculously, I still got my Ph.D. I was 43. I knew I might be too old. I knew my research and statistics were a joke, I would never be an Ivy League professor constantly publishing amazing papers. But there was one thing I could hold on to: I could teach. I might not be the teacher of the year, but teaching could be my career. In America.

Then I landed a job at a small university in New Mexico.

I got the opportunity to teach statistics and research. Then I learned something interesting: when you have to teach something, suddenly your mind is clearer about it. I picked up a statistics book and carefully read through it, imagining how I would teach it to students. It worked. I was able to grasp some simple and basic concepts. Still insufficient, but good enough to teach lower and middle levels. As for research, this small school doesn’t have enough resources for me to conduct research/gather data on a large scale, therefore no publication for me. But I LOVE working with students and mentoring them on their research projects. My students and I have traveled (for free, that’s the best part) to places, e.g., Portland, San Antonio, Pasadena for conferences; we enjoy ourselves in these beautiful cities’ attractions and presenting the results we’re proud of. There’s no big published study under my name, but that’s good enough for me. 

If you’re unsure of yourself, maybe my story can help a little.

Know who you are and what you can do: it greatly impacts your goals and thus your future. You might not know everything, you might not be perfect, you might have an intense fear of the unknown—but if it’s worth it, keep moving forward. I didn’t dare to even dream about what I’m doing right now, but I knew I was eager for knowledge, I always saw myself as an intellectual, or at least trying to be.

But keep in mind: focus on manifesting your potential instead of big money or fame. Pursuing growth instead of material things. Remember: things you can touch will NEVER last. If my goal were fortune or power, I can guarantee I’d have failed and I’d have never been happy.

People may doubt you. In fact, if no one ever doubts you, your dream might not be big enough. If I die tomorrow, I’ll have a lot of regrets due to my many shortcomings and bad breath, but at least I’ll have some comfort: for my whole life, I’ve more than once proved many doubters/haters wrong and shut their mouths. I fucking LOVE doing that.    

I’m nobody, my story isn’t as inspirational as Diana Trujillo’s; far from it—I’m just a gnat compared to her. I still don’t know how to small talk or chit-chat, my kids always make fun of my accent, I constantly misspell words, and I have a hard time understanding how committees in school work. But I’ve proved myself just a little in my own way. As I look back to where I started, I think I can say to myself: yeah, sometimes, just sometimes, I’m fucking awesome.

And you can prove yourself in your own way too.

items.content_html:
Chapter 1

Orion woke and immediately touched his forehead. Huh, I’m alive... wait, I’m standing? Looking around, he realized he was in the middle of a narrow street. It was a dark night, with a dim, yellowish streetlight in the distance casting blurry shadows on the trees lining the road. The air felt somehow cold, as it had just rained. The road was still wet, and water was dripping from the leaves.

How did I get here? It took him a while to concentrate. Wait, I remember someone pointing a gun at me; then something hit my forehead like I’d been kicked by a horse… He touched his forehead again: it was smooth and dry, with no hole or blood. Who was it? It had felt like a bullet drilled into my head… He felt his arms, hands, legs, and toes. Everything was fine.  

This unpaved street was in the middle of nowhere; no houses or buildings were in sight, not even a stop sign or speed limit. Not knowing what else to do, he started walking. The sound of his footsteps on the dirt and small rocks scratched into the eerie silence.

A car approached from behind, but he didn’t look. When the car slowly passed him, his peripheral vision caught a glimpse of a young kid in the passenger seat looking at him funny.

He walked for about half an hour before seeing some dingy wooden houses on the left. They were old and run-down, with broken doorsteps and cracked windows. A bit further, some people were lounging, smoking, or talking around a fire. They were all in thick coats. They became quiet when he walked near them, staring at him as though seeing a ghost.

He didn’t know why, but he felt compelled to keep walking.

There were more run-down houses and ragged people. A group of three glared in his direction, then the one with a beard coughed. They walked up to block his way. “Hey bro, what’s up?” the bearded one said.

“Not much,” Orion replied. A hint of foul smell mixing tobacco, cheap booze, and other nameless sour odors like sweat dried in the sun found its way to his nose.

“You ain’t cold? What are you doing out so late around here?”

“I don’t know.”

They looked at each other and smirked. “Alright, you got some cash? My bro here needs a few dimes for his child support, you know what it’s like.”

Orion knew this was a robbery, but a strange calmness lodged in his chest, or maybe a lack of emotions. He searched his pocket, fished out his wallet, and opened it. “Sorry, no cash.”

“Plastic will do, too,” the bearded man laughed.

“But that’s mine.”

“You sure about that?” Another guy with a tattoo of a dragon on his right forearm pulled out a big knife.

Orion shrugged.

“Oh,” they acted surprised, looked at each other and laughed. The third guy, who had two nose rings, said, “So you wanna play it the hard way, huh? Tough guy?”

People started gathering. “Give them what they want, it’s not worth it,” some guy shouted.

“Listen to them, bro,” the bearded man said.

Orion put his wallet back into his pocket.

The tattooed guy pointed that big knife right at Orion’s face, only two inches away from his nose. “Give.”

Why isn’t my heart pounding? Shouldn’t I be scared? Orion replied, “We don’t have to do this… how about I buy you drinks? Dinner?”   

“Shut the fuck up and give me the fucking wallet,” the tattooed guy said in a low, threatening voice. “Another word and you’ll be crying for your mommy.”

“Listen…”

The knife slashed through Orion’s right arm, from bicep to wrist. Some among the crowd screamed. Then absolute silence.

“How…” The tattooed guy’s eyes grew big. Orion looked at his right arm, then looked up at the three guys; his face turned a little paler with more puzzlement.

“You didn’t cut him?” the nose ring guy asked.

“I did, I did, I…” The tattooed guy was shaking a little, then yelled, “Fuck!” and slashed across Orion’s right arm and his abdomen. It should have cut his stomach open.

The shirt tore, but his belly was untouched.

“Fuck! What’s this shit? Fuck you!” the tattooed guy shrieked at the top of his lungs, “I’m gonna kill you! You creep! Die now! Die!” he stabbed Orion in the chest five times, ten times, fifteen times… After he had stopped stabbing, Orion just stood there looking at him. The tattooed guy was panting and trembling.

“This is fucking creepy…” a voice came from the crowd. “Fuck this shit, I’m out of here!” Suddenly everyone started screaming and scattered. Orion was alone with his long ghostly shadow.

The next morning at around seven.

The sun's rays began to break through the clouds, painting the sky orange and yellow. A small restaurant, Green Creek, had a few guests enjoying their scrambled eggs and coffee. A young waitress was taking orders. The smell of freshly fried bacon and waffles wafted nearly two blocks away, drawing a few stray dogs and cats to linger nearby.

A bald middle-aged man with a mustache was sipping his coffee when he saw a miserable-looking man open the door. It was Orion. This was mid-December, but he only wore a torn navy blue short-sleeve shirt that barely held together, and a pair of jeans. Some frost formed on the tips of his hair. He didn’t seem cold though. The bald man stopped sipping.

Orion found a seat near him and sat down. Everyone in the restaurant couldn’t help but stare. The waitress very slowly walked up to Orion’s table.

“Can I have a cup of coffee and a shepherd’s pie?” Orion said.

“Sure… you okay, sir? Do you need anything? A blanket maybe?” the waitress asked.

“No, I’m fine; thank you for asking,” he grinned. Maybe the grin was to be reassuring, but everyone felt their hair standing up.

She poured a cup of coffee for him and slowly walked away, still looking at him.

A few more guests came in. The noise of people chatting, the busboy collecting plates and utensils, and the occasional clanking from the kitchen grew louder and more expansive, yet Orion’s attention stayed on his exposed torso, eyes drifting downward as he continued to feel it.

“Hey, sir,” the bald man said. “Wanna sit with me?”

Orion kept on touching his own chest, seeming distracted and disturbed.

“Sir?”

Orion raised his head, “Yes, sorry?”

“You want to sit here?” the bald man pointed at the seat across from him.   

(To be continued)

items.title: Sexual Infidelity: What Are the Predictors, According to Research?

items.content_html:
What kinds of people/situations are more likely to lead to affairs?

When I was a young teen, I already had a clear idea of what I’d do if my future spouse cheated on me: divorce. No other alternative. However, as I grew older, had my own family, have seen more, I gradually realized the issue was way more complicated than I’d believed.

There are, of course, tons of studies on this topic. What I’m going to do here is just review some quick summaries, and I’ll only focus on the most “stereotypical” type: sexual infidelity.

But first, how prevalent is it? It’s not that easy to find out the exact number because few people will be willing to openly admit it. In general, research suggests that it’s around 20 – 25% in America (for example, see here and here); in other words, one in about four to five people will have sex with someone other than their spouse/partner at least once. Dr. Mark at Indiana University and her colleagues stated that infidelity is the most common reason for divorce in America, and Dr. Betzig at the University of Michigan also claimed that it’s the #1 reason in at least 160 other countries. Guess too many people think with that thing between their legs and their spouses aren’t happy about it.

Dr. Atkins, a clinical psychologist at the University of Washington, and his colleagues analyzed a big data set from national surveys of around 4,000 people. Let’s break down the findings into different categories.

Demographic factors

Men vs. Women  

Yes, according to this study, men are more likely to have sexual affairs than women. But what’s more interesting is the probability changes throughout different ages: men between the ages of 55 and 65 at the time of the survey are the most likely to report infidelity (about 15%). Is it because men who reach these ages typically have the itch? Or because of the “cohort effect,” which means these male respondents grew up in a certain culture that somehow “encourages” infidelity? We don’t really know, but the researchers infer it’s because of the cohort effect.

Women have a much lower probability (around 4 – 5%), and they’re more likely to report infidelity between the ages of 40 and 45. Again, this might NOT be saying women of these ages want to have affairs; it might be the effect of the culture experienced in this particular age group, we don’t really know.

However, this study as well as Dr. Fincham at Florida State University and his colleague also pointed out that this gap between men and women is closing. Women nowadays represent a significant part of the workforce, which means they have more financial power, independence, and opportunity for infidelity.  

Education

Respondents with graduate degrees AND who have previously divorced are 1.75 times more likely to have affairs (again) than those with less than high school diplomas. The study didn’t say much about possible reasons, my guess is that these people are more likely to have status and opportunity.

Religion

People who report attending church regularly AND are highly satisfied with their marriages (reporting “very happy”) have a lower likelihood of infidelity. For those who attend church regularly but report marriage satisfaction as “pretty happy” or “not too happy,” their religious behavior isn’t associated with any lower probability of infidelity.

Looking at what other studies find, we know that religion is a complicated factor. The study in 2007 must be loved by many faithful church-goers: they found that people who see the Bible as the literal word of God are significantly less likely to have affairs. On the other hand, however, this study by Iranian researchers in 2019 and Dr. Mark’s research found no such relationship.

I think maybe one reason for the big discrepancy is that people attend church for a variety of motives. Some truly internalize the values of religious teaching, while others go to the chapel just because that’s another place to talk and maybe eat, but the surveys might have a harder time catching that. Just my speculation though.

History of divorce

Yup, people who’ve divorced before are nearly twice as likely to have affairs again than those who’ve never divorced.

Incomes/employment status

The study put incomes and employment status together as an indicator of opportunity. For incomes, among people who make $30,000/year or more (about $45,755 in 2021, see this calculator), the more they make the more likelihood of having affairs. No such relationship among people making less than $30,000. It’s suggested that with higher incomes, people might have higher status and more opportunities for traveling or seeing new people. Also, they didn’t ask the incomes of more than $75,000/year (about $114,386 in 2021); they thought that maybe for crazy-rich people the relationship would be even stronger.  

For employment status, they have four categories: respondents and their spouses both are employed, respondents and their spouses both are unemployed, respondents are employed but their spouses aren’t, and respondents aren’t employed but their spouses are. The “respondents are employed but their spouses aren’t” category is the most likely to have affairs—probably because this signifies the most power difference. The “both are unemployed” is the least likely to have affairs, guess they don’t have the time, energy, or chance.

Age of first marriage

The younger the people got married the first time, the more likely they’ll have affairs. Those who were first married at 16 (goodness) are almost 4 times more likely to have affairs than people at 23. This is expected: if you ask me, teens are, in general, impulsive, immature, and not experienced. When I was a teen I was stupid like hell, can’t imagine what would have happened if I were married at 16.

Relationship

Relationship satisfaction

People might think only those who are in unhappy marriages will go out and seek alternatives, but the researchers of this study reviewed the literature and found that some studies indicated no such relationship. Some, however, did suggest that inadequate marital qualities, e.g., low relationship satisfaction and low frequency of sex were quite significant predictors of infidelity. One of the purposes of this study was to find out which side is supported in the population they studied. And they found it: the data analyses indicated that compared to those who report “very happy” in their relationship, people who report “pretty happy” are almost 2 times more likely to have affairs, and people who report “not too happy” are 4 times more likely. Further, researchers at Pennsylvania State University suggested that low marital satisfaction can both be the cause and the consequence of infidelity.  

Note: this is by no means an excuse for affairs (“I have an affair because I’m not happy in my relationship!”); for one thing, this unhappy relationship might be your fault. It’s rarely only one partner’s fault anyway.

Commitment

In terms of relationship satisfaction, Dr. Drigotas, a psychologist at Johns Hopkins University, along with his colleagues stated that commitment is one crucial key to higher satisfaction, which predicts a lower probability of infidelity. People with a stronger commitment have higher attachment and desire to continue the relationships.

Further, people who cohabit before marriage are more likely to have affairs (for example, see this study). I think “commitment” might explain why: the idea of cohabitation is “let’s try and see if this works,” which implies a lack of commitment.  

Therefore, it seems that for a relationship to work well, both have to be committed.

Besides these factors above reviewed by Dr. Atkins and his colleagues, Dr. Fincham and his colleagues also summarized some other factors. 

Similarities

According to research, “opposites attract” doesn’t work in long-term relationships. Interestingly, according to Drs. Brooks and Monaco, the economists at the University of Wisconsin at LaCrosse, couples who are devoted to the same religion and have higher levels of education have lower probabilities of infidelity. In general, these two factors are people’s core values, and it’s hard to stay with someone with different core values.

Personality/individual

Neuroticism

People who are neurotic (emotionally unstable, prone to negative emotions such as anger, anxiety, depression; for example, see this study) are more likely to have affairs. As you can see, neurotic individuals are not happy people.  

Attachment styles

An insecure attachment style is associated with higher chances of infidelity, but this study doesn’t specify which style. Luckily, psychologists at Florida State University found that those higher in anxiety attachment are more likely to have affairs.  

Attachment styles are too huge a topic to explain here, I’ll go into details in another article. Basically, anxious style individuals are always highly on guard for the relationship, constantly worry that they’re not good enough and therefore will be abandoned; they’re those who are clingy to their partners. Strange and counter-intuitive, right? If you’re afraid to be abandoned, why would you go find someone else? We’ll talk about it in another piece.

Behavioral problems

Drug/alcohol abuse is positively related to infidelity; the more use of drugs, the higher chance of infidelity.

Attitude toward sex

Yup, of course: those who can “separate sex from love,” those who see casual sex as no big deal are more likely to f*k someone else.

Family of origin

An individual’s parent(s) have an impact too. Those who see parental infidelity are twice more likely to do it themselves than those who don’t have parental infidelity. It can be “monkey see, monkey do,” but the reasons might be way more complicated than that.

Internet

Oh yeah, the internet is another whole new world, isn’t it? This study said that 20 – 33% of people use the internet for sex, and among these people, 65% do it. To make it worse, more than half of them engage in unprotected sex. This has become a problem of spreading STDs and HIV, and therefore a costly issue for public health.

POTENTIAL APPLICATION

Okay, at this point, some of you might be getting nervous: oh no, I/my partner got many of these factors, are we doomed?

Dr. Atkins advised not to panic because of the nature of the research: this study, along with all related investigations, is correlational. In other words, they only examine relationships, not cause-and-effect. If we can gather a bunch of married people in a huge lab, randomly assign them to the “opportunity” group with many other potential sexual partners, and the “no opportunity” group with no potential sexual partners (maybe very old people?), then see what will happen in maybe three years, then we might establish cause-and-effect on whether the opportunity factor is indeed a cause. That sounds like fun, but we can’t do that.

Correlation is not causation, so we have to be careful when we interpret these findings.

However, they still offered some potential suggestions. First, because the combination of one working and one staying home is the most vulnerable type to infidelity,

…couples with one working partner might give particular attention to how to maintain a sense of equality in power and control in the marriage and develop strategies to interact with other individuals and couples together.

They also recommended couples keep working on their relationships to achieve high standards of “very happy” and high satisfaction.   

And finally, these are my takeaways. From what I’ve seen, infidelity is complicated, and sometimes it’s not necessarily 100% the fault of the one who commits adultery, but the consequence is damaging. In many cases, it doesn’t only end in divorce but much farther and longer. In general, to prevent heartbreaks, commitment is the key, as Dr. Digotas’s research indicated. It can be a little like choosing a career: you don’t jump around whenever you see problems.  

And to be able to commit, a shared, common goal or goals is a vital component. I read somewhere about this: “Love is not only in couple looking at each other, but also in them looking toward the same direction” or words to that effect.

On the other hand, however, some infidelity is from much deeper and troublesome underlying problems, e.g., addiction, mental health issues, or even abuse. They have to be addressed before any reconciliation can happen, and maybe these people need a little more empathetic eye.

items.title: To Combat Inflammation in My Body, I Eat Two Superfoods and Avoid Three
